article.title: The Glovebox Checklist
article.author: Britta Hedlund
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Most drivers keep registration papers and a few random receipts in the glovebox, but little for the minutes after a collision. Your phone battery might be low, the other driver may be upset, and important details can be easy to forget when you’re shaken. A small, organized kit can help you contact people, document the scene, and keep essential information together. It won’t prevent a crash, but it can make the aftermath easier to manage. Quick Overview: Keep insurance documents, emergency contacts, a charged phone, basic safety supplies, and an evidence checklist in your car. After a collision, prioritize safety, seek medical care when needed, and record important details promptly. The 10 Essentials to Keep in Your Car You don’t need a bulky emergency kit. A few carefully chosen items can help you stay safe, exchange information, and handle unexpected delays. Keep them organized and check them every few months. 1. Proof of Insurance and Vehicle Registration Keep current proof of insurance and vehicle registration easy to reach. Digital copies can help, but make sure you can access them if your phone loses power or service. Having these documents ready makes exchanging information with another driver or speaking with responding officers easier. 2. A Phone Charger or Power Bank Your phone may be your camera, flashlight, map, and way to contact help. Keep a compatible car charger or charged power bank with the necessary cable. Check the battery periodically so it’s ready when needed, especially if your vehicle’s electrical system is damaged in a collision. 3. Emergency Contacts and a Medical Information Card Keep a printed emergency contact list and a small medical information card in a protected sleeve. Include relevant allergies, medications, and conditions emergency personnel may need to know. Limit sensitive details to what’s useful, and store the card securely in case you cannot communicate clearly after a crash. 4. A Pen and Small Notebook Phones can fail, so keep a pen and notebook handy. Use them to record names, license plates, witness contacts, the location, weather, and any police report number. Write down what happened while your memory is fresh, sticking to observations rather than guesses about who caused the collision. 5. A Flashlight A compact flashlight helps you find documents and see your surroundings after dark. Check its batteries regularly. Using a separate light also preserves your phone battery for calls and photographs. Never step into traffic or approach damaged vehicles in an unsafe position just to get a better look. 6. Reflective Triangles or Roadside Warning Devices Reflective triangles can warn approaching drivers about a stopped vehicle, particularly on busy roads or after dark. Store them securely and learn how to use them beforehand. Only place warning devices when it’s safe; don’t walk into moving traffic or put yourself at risk to set them out. 7. A Basic First-Aid Kit Keep bandages, disposable gloves, gauze, and antiseptic wipes for minor injuries. A first-aid kit is not a substitute for medical care. For serious bleeding, suspected head or neck injuries, or other emergencies, contact emergency services and follow their instructions rather than attempting treatment beyond your training. 8. A Blanket and Bottled Water Waiting for roadside assistance can take longer than expected. A compact blanket helps in cold weather, while bottled water can be useful during a delay in warm conditions. Check stored water periodically and replace it as needed. Depending on the season, consider adding gloves or other practical supplies. 9. A Checklist of Photos to Take Once everyone is safe, use a checklist to document the scene. Photograph each vehicle from several angles, license plates, visible damage, road signs, traffic signals, weather, and relevant debris or skid marks. Don’t delay medical care or put yourself in danger to take pictures. 10. A List of Details to Collect Keep a printed checklist of details to exchange with the other driver and, where relevant, responding officers. Record names, contact details, insurance company and policy information, license plates, vehicle descriptions, witness contacts, and the officer’s name or report number. Insurance matters because not every driver has coverage. The Insurance Information Institute reports that 15.4% of U.S. motorists were uninsured in 2023, according to a 2025 Insurance Research Council study. Its uninsured motorist statistics explain why documenting insurance information and knowing your own coverage can matter. After the Kit Has Done Its Job Once everyone is safe, call 911 if anyone is injured or there’s an immediate hazard. Follow emergency responders’ instructions and request a police report when appropriate. Notify your insurer promptly, describe what you know, and avoid guessing about fault. Seek medical attention if you’re hurt or concerned about possible injuries, even if you initially feel fine. Symptoms of injuries such as whiplash or concussion may appear later. If discomfort develops days after the collision, this guide explains considerations around reporting an injury after a crash. Keep medical records, repair estimates, receipts, photographs, and insurance correspondence together. Organized records make it easier to answer questions later without relying entirely on memory. When a Lawyer Is Worth a Call Legal guidance may be useful when someone is injured, fault is disputed, the other driver appears uninsured, or an insurer requests a recorded statement or proposes a quick settlement before the full impact of the crash is clear. Your notes, photographs, witness details, and insurance information can help an attorney understand the circumstances. For drivers involved in a Chicago-area collision, the car accident attorneys at Chicago Auto Injury Lawyers can provide information about potential next steps. Ten minutes of preparation can make a stressful situation easier to manage. Assemble your kit, check it a few times a year, and replace anything that expires or runs out.
